_meta.addresses_reviewer: R3 (round 1, arXiv v1) — random bytes are the wrong workload for an encoding detector

metrics_glossary.exact_match_rate: fraction of inputs where v6.detect(x) == v7.detect(x) as Python dicts (exact equality, including the literal encoding label string and the floating-point confidence)
metrics_glossary.bucket_match_rate: fraction where (encoding, confidence-bucket) matches; bucket = high>=0.9 / med>=0.5 / low<0.5 / none if missing
metrics_glossary.normalized_match_rate: as bucket_match_rate but with the encoding label case-folded, common aliases collapsed (cp1252==windows-1252, cp932==shift_jis, gb2312==gb18030, ...) and ascii/windows-1252/iso-8859-1 collapsed at high confidence (ASCII bytes decode identically through all three). This isolates `different decoder picked` from `same decoder, different label`.

_meta.note_on_exact_match_zero: All buckets show exact_match_rate=0 because v7 reformats encoding labels (lowercase canonical names: 'windows-1252', 'cp932', 'gb18030') where v6 emitted uppercase aliases ('WINDOWS-1252', 'SHIFT_JIS', 'GB18030'). The exact_match metric is therefore a label-format probe more than a decoder probe in this dataset. The bucket and normalized rates are the operationally interesting metrics.

aggregate_excluding_random_control._comment: the operationally interesting headline: realistic-input agreement on the 64 non-random items

html_latin.notes: Disagreement on the 2/4 misses is v6 calling Wikipedia article bytes 'ascii' (high confidence) while v7 calls them 'utf-8' (high confidence). The Wikipedia pages are technically UTF-8 (declared in <meta charset>) but the leading 8 KiB are ASCII-only. v7 picks up the declaration; v6 picks up the byte distribution. Both are defensible reads.

html_cjk.notes: Perfect bucket agreement: both v6 and v7 identify the Chinese, Japanese, and Korean Wikipedia HTML as UTF-8 at high confidence. The exact_match miss is the label-case mismatch.

rfc_ascii.notes: Sharp divergence: v6 cleanly identifies all four RFC bodies as ASCII at confidence 1.0. v7 identifies them as 'cp864' (an obscure Arabic codepage) at confidence 0.22..0.55. This is a notable regression — v7's ML-assisted classifier picks an exotic Arabic-domain codepage over the obvious ASCII answer on pure 7-bit text. The RFCs are well below 100 KB so 'too little text' is not the explanation; v6 is right.

email_mime.notes: After label normalisation v6 and v7 agree on 5/7 MIME messages. The two genuine disagreements are an ASCII English body (v6: ascii / v7: Windows-1252 — operationally equivalent on this content) and a GB18030 Chinese body (v6: 0.99 confidence GB18030 / v7: 0.70 confidence gb18030 — same decoder, lower v7 confidence drops it to a different bucket).

multilingual_utf8.notes: Strong agreement on multilingual UTF-8 — 8/9 normalised matches across en/fr/de/es/zh/ja/ko/ru/ar. The lone disagreement is the French UDHR text, where v6 reports utf-8 at 0.99 (high bucket) and v7 reports utf-8 at 0.83 (med bucket): same decoder, different confidence.

multilingual_gb18030.notes: Sharp divergence on GB18030. Only the Chinese-language input is identified by both versions (and v7 with weaker confidence). v6 misidentifies the Russian-in-GB18030 text as Big5; v7 misidentifies the Korean and Russian variants as cp862 and cp720. Both detectors struggle here because GB18030 is variable-length and the inputs are short; the disagreement pattern shows the two classifiers' priors are different.

multilingual_shiftjis.notes: After collapsing the cp932 / SHIFT_JIS alias and the ascii / Windows-1252 superset, both Shift_JIS samples agree.

multilingual_windows1252.notes: Both versions correctly identify Windows-1252 (or ascii for the English variant). 0/4 strict bucket matches collapses to 4/4 once the case-fold and ascii/Windows-1252 collapse are applied — this bucket is the clearest illustration that v1's exact_match metric was a label-format probe.

multilingual_iso88591.notes: Same story as multilingual_windows1252: both detectors converge on Windows-1252 (which is a strict superset of ISO-8859-1; chardet has historically not distinguished the two), and the strict bucket misses are entirely the v6 'WINDOWS-1252' vs v7 'windows-1252' label-case difference.

short_snippets.notes: On the < 100-byte regime where the detector has minimal signal, v6 and v7 agree on the easy cases (BOMs, pure ASCII, longer CJK strings) and disagree on the short Latin-1 / Windows-1252 fragments. v7's confidences are markedly lower (0.07..0.14) on the short Latin-1 samples than v6's (0.59..0.71), suggesting v7 has been calibrated to be more cautious in the data-starved regime.

malformed.notes: Mojibake / mixed-encoding inputs produce the most varied disagreement: v7 picks exotic codepages (cp874, iso-8859-4, Windows-1255) where v6 settles on Windows-1252. Neither is 'right' — these inputs are by construction undecidable — but the disagreement pattern shows the two classifiers' tie-breaking heuristics diverged.

random_control.notes: Identical to the v1 number (the v1 corpus is preserved here as the random_control bucket). v6 returns {encoding: None, confidence: 0.0} on essentially every random byte string; v7 returns {encoding: None, confidence: 0.95} — the format of v7's 'I don't know' response changed (a high-confidence null encoding rather than a zero-confidence null encoding). This alone destroys the strict bucket-match metric in the random regime.

c06e.headline_finding: On random bytes (v1's only workload) v6 and v7 are fully diverged. On realistic input — Wikipedia HTML, RFC bodies, multilingual plain text, MIME messages — once encoding-label normalisation is applied the two versions agree on the decoder family 62.5% of the time (40/64 non-random items). The genuine behavioural divergences are concentrated in (a) ASCII vs Windows-1252 superset boundary, (b) v7's 'cp864' label on pure ASCII RFCs (a notable regression), (c) confidence calibration in the data-starved short-snippet regime, and (d) the random-input null-response format. Conclusion: the operational contract is partially preserved on realistic input (62.5% normalised agreement) but with a non-trivial set of edge-case regressions; the v1 paper's 'fully diverged on random fuzz' framing was correct in its narrow domain but understated the realistic-input agreement.

v2_paper_c06e_numbers.corpus: 11 realistic-input buckets + 1 random-bytes control bucket; see corpora/MANIFEST.tsv

comparison_appendix.compatibility_note: The v1 number (0/0 on 1000 random inputs) is exactly reproduced inside the v2 corpus as the random_control bucket. The v2 paper does not contradict the v1 paper — it just adds realistic-input rows the v1 paper omitted.
